```{r}
  c("(n = 1438)", "85% (n = 1438) of archived data had a licence", { k <- sum(arch_d & coop$data_license %in% c("Yes", "Yes, but not for all data archived")); paste(pct(k, 1690), k) }),
  c("(n = 1076)", "CC0 (n = 1076) for data", sum(arch_d & coop$data_license_type %in% "CC0")),
  c("(n = 457)", "79% (n = 457) of archived code had a DOI", { k <- sum(arch_c & coop$code_doi %in% c("Yes", "Yes, same as data")); paste(pct(k, 577), k) }),
  c("(n = 428)", "74% (n = 428) of archived code had a licence", { k <- sum(arch_c & coop$code_license %in% "Yes"); paste(pct(k, 577), k) }),
  c("(n = 122)", "CC BY (n = 122) for code", sum(arch_c & coop$code_license_type %in% "CC BY")),
  c("(n = 104)", "CC0 (n = 104) for code", sum(arch_c & coop$code_license_type %in% "CC0")),
  c("Handle", "4 Handle links, 3 Figshare, 1 Arctic, 2 archives", "Read in the audit rows: entry C5.15"),
  c("over 90%", "over 90% of 66 repositories", "COAR report: entry C5.8")
)
typed <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, typed))
typed <- data.frame(Where = vapply(typed[[1]], where_now, ""), `As stated` = typed[[2]], `Recomputed or found` = typed[[3]], check.names = FALSE)
typed[2:3] <- lapply(typed[2:3], esc)
md_table(typed, c(16, 40, 40))
```

The column "Where" is found again at every render, by searching the manuscript for the number. On 10 November 2026, eleven typed numbers that this table listed on 1 November were no longer in the manuscript, because the sentences holding them had been removed (the earlier history of defects in the Discussion, the abstract's estimates of 24 minutes and 2 to 25 hours, and the account of the 16 repositories and the 38 flagged repositories); they are no longer listed. The value 543, the number of papers rated on annotation, is now computed in the text and so appears in Part 1. The recomputed percentages are rounded to whole numbers, as in Cooper et al.'s text. All values Cooper et al. report that were tested here follow from their public file, with two points worth noting. Their 57% for Dryad and the percentages beside it are shares of the 1782 platform labels on the 1670 papers with a coded platform, not shares of papers. Their 61% for README on code counts only papers coded as archiving code; without that restriction the count would be 353.

Typed numbers that are not quantities (such as "Appendix A.5", "version 0.3.3.9" or "the two sides") were not listed. Typed numbers that describe facts about the project, such as "Twelve" defects and "seven" fixes, are treated as statements in Part 2 (entries C18.1 and C18.5).

# Part 2: Register of factual statements

The entries follow the order of the manuscript as it was on 1 November 2026. Quotations give the words tested, and line numbers refer to `documentation/manuscript.qmd` as it was then. The current line of each quotation, and whether the entry has since been resolved, are given in the tables of the Summary of results. Cooper et al. (2026) was read in the published version, from the open copy in the NERC Open Research Archive (<https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/541841/1/N541841JA.pdf>). Where an entry says "the protocol", it means their Supporting Information A, `documentation/cooper_supplement_documentation.pdf`.

## Title page and abstract

**C1.1 — QUALIFIED.** Line 36: "even the lightest form of computational reproducibility checking ... has been estimated to take around 24 minutes per article, and writing independent analysis code from scratch has been estimated at 2-25 person-hours per article." Both figures can be traced: 24 minutes is the mean time reported by Obels et al. (2020) for registered reports in psychology, and 2 to 25 person-hours is an estimate from Hardwicke et al. (2018) as cited there. The Sage page refused automated access, so this rests on a search result quoting the article, not on a reading of it. The abstract gives no citation, although `obels2020` is in `references.bib`. **Correction:** cite both, and state that 24 minutes refers to psychology papers whose code ran. "Lightest form" is a judgement of the authors.

**C1.2 — TRUE.** Line 36: Cooper et al. "manually coded data- and code-archiving practices in 1861 papers published across the seven British Ecological Society (BES) journals between 2017 and 2024". Their abstract says the same, and the public file has 1861 rows, seven journals and years 2017 to 2024. The 1861 are about 20% of the 8112 eligible papers (Cooper et al., p. 1958), which the manuscript does not mention and could.

**C1.3 — TRUE.** Line 36: "a two-day hackathon of 145 participants who followed a bespoke coding protocol". Cooper et al., p. 1956: "a hackathon event (29-30th September 2025), where 145 (in-person and online) participants ... followed a bespoke protocol". Column `recorder_ID` has 145 values. The protocol allowed work outside these two days, and one ID can be a group: "each unique data recorder, or group of data recorders, was given a recorder ID number". "145 participants" is therefore Cooper et al.'s number, whereas line 328's "145 people coded" should read "145 recorders" (see C2.19).

**C1.4 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 36: tools extract this information "in a fraction of the time". No comparison of time is reported. Metacheck's run took many hours, and the coders' total time is not recorded. The claim is plausible but has no measurement behind it.

**C1.5 — TRUE.** Line 36: "We ran Metacheck's `repo_check`, `data_check`, and `code_check` modules on the same corpus". The results file holds all three for 1861 papers, with no errors recorded (`errors` has no rows). `code/run_metacheck.R` also runs three further modules.

**C1.6 — TRUE.** Line 36: compared "for every construct where a direct, mechanical comparison is possible: data availability, archive location, data licensing, data and code download success, code archiving, and README presence". These are the eight entries of `results`. File format (`mc_data_format`) and language (`mc_code_language`) could also be compared mechanically and are not, so "every" is slightly too strong. No change is needed unless a reader asks.

**C1.7 — QUALIFIED.** Line 36: "For each construct we report sensitivity, specificity, and two directional miss rates". The summary table does so for six constructs. For archive location it leaves these columns empty, because the comparison there is of sets. **Correction:** "for each construct with a yes or no answer".

**C1.8 — QUALIFIED.** Line 36: "we individually reviewed every disagreeing paper against Metacheck's saved output, the paper's own text, and, where relevant, a live call to the repository platform's own API". All 876 rows carry verdicts on every disagreeing column. However, of 1216 verdicts, only 21 are stamped with the version of the final run. The others were written against earlier versions and carried forward when both answers stayed the same (see C9.7). The reader should know that "saved output" often means the output of an earlier run.

**C1.9 — TRUE.** Line 36: the five agreement percentages, 99.2, 99.8, 85.5, 87.9 and 72.9. These are typed by hand and match the computed values (Part 1). One caution: "whether data could be downloaded and used" at 99.2% is limited to papers where Metacheck saved a data file. Over all papers the coders downloaded, it is 83.6%, as line 801 reports. An abstract that gives only the first figure flatters the tool. **Suggested addition:** give both.

**C1.10 — QUALIFIED.** Line 36: "Metacheck's precision is consistently high across constructs". Positive predictive value is above 96% for five constructs and 91.9% for code archiving, as the manuscript itself reports at line 1021. "Consistently" should be "high for five of six constructs". Precision here means agreement with the coders.

**C1.11 — TRUE.** Line 36: recall is driven by "at least one genuine definitional mismatch (platform-level description metadata a human coder reasonably reads as README-equivalent, which Metacheck's stricter file-presence check does not)". This agrees with Cooper et al.'s question and, since the reclassification of 1 November 2026, with the body of the manuscript (C12.4, C12.9). The 294 such papers count as misses in the sensitivity of 64.2%.

**C1.12 — TRUE.** Line 36: the causes of low recall include "a real, working data or code citation on a platform or in a format Metacheck does not yet recognise" and "data or code shared in a form that does not identify it as data or code". The audit supports both: 101 papers on unsupported FAIR platforms and 26 with files not classified.

**C1.13 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 36: "Our goal is not to replace manual coding". This is a statement of intent.

**C1.14 — QUALIFIED.** Line 20: "A reproducible version of this manuscript is available at https://github.com/Lakens/cooper-bes-validation." That repository exists and is public, but it is the earlier one. The final repository is `Lakens/bes_validation`, which is private at the time of checking. **Correction:** change the address and make the repository public at submission.

**C1.15 — QUALIFIED.** Line 19: "The author has no conflict of interest to declare." The manuscript evaluates Metacheck, and the author is one of its four named authors (`R-metacheck` in `package_citations.bib`). This is not a financial conflict, as far as can be seen from the repository, but a reader would want to know. **Correction:** declare that the author is a developer of the tool.

## Introduction

**C2.1 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 322: "The last two decades has seen a notable culture change around open science practices. Universities, journals, and funders increasingly expect researchers to engage in open science practices." No citation is given. It is a widely held view but should be supported with a reference. The verb should be "have seen".

**C2.2 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 322: "One open science practice that has become especially widely required is data and code sharing. The goal ... is to facilitate re-use, and to increase transparency." No citation is given. Cooper et al. (p. 1955) describes the same goals and can be cited.

**C2.3 — UNVERIFIED.** Line 322: "Funders have started to require data management plans ... and submission guidelines for journals often require that data and code ... are shared if possible." This is common knowledge in the field, but no source is given and none was checked here. A citation of one funder's policy and one journal policy study would settle it. **Author's decision (10 November 2026):** the general statement is true, but no scoping review covers the requirements of both funders and journals over the last 20 years. Any citation would be more specific than the claim and would not fully support it, so the sentence is kept without a citation.

**C2.4 — UNVERIFIED.** Line 322: the quotation from the BES author guidelines, "all data and code supporting the results in the paper must be archived in a public repository". The page refused automated access (HTTP 403), and a search found no copy of this sentence. The policy described by Cooper et al. (p. 1955) is narrower for code: data archiving has been mandatory "at all seven journals since January 2014", and "code-archiving has been required for papers presenting simulations, new applications and non-standard analyses since 2017 (2015 for MEE)". **To settle:** open the page in a browser and compare the sentence, including whether the rule has changed since the corpus years. If it has, note that the corpus was published under the narrower rule.

**C2.5 — QUALIFIED.** Line 324: "it is less clear who is responsible to check that authors actually follow through". Cooper et al. (p. 1955) states that "journal staff check each accepted paper to ensure authors have archived data and code according to BES editorial policies", but "do not have the skills or capacity to guarantee" completeness and reusability. The manuscript's sentence is fair for quality but too strong for presence. **Correction:** cite that passage.

**C2.6 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 324: "Manually checking data and code files is a time-consuming task that requires expertise". This agrees with Cooper et al. on skills, and with Obels et al. on time.

**C2.7 — FALSE.** Line 324: "Due to the diffusion of responsibility and the lack of resources ... requirements to share data and code are often not followed". Two parts fail. For data, Cooper et al. found the reverse, 97% archived (p. 1958), and describes "high compliance". And no evidence in the manuscript or cited work shows the cause, diffusion of responsibility. The sentence is true for code (35%). **Correction:** "requirements to share code are often not followed, and shared data and code often do not follow best practices", and drop the causal phrase or mark it as a suggestion.

**C2.8 — TRUE.** Line 324: Cooper et al. "assessed data- and code-archiving practices across the seven journals", and "most manuscripts in which data was used also shared the data, but code sharing was less common". The figures are 97% and 35% (p. 1958).

**C2.9 — TRUE.** Line 324: "About a third of data and/or code repositories lacked a README file". Cooper et al., p. 1961: "around a third of papers lacked a README or similar". The manuscript's review shows many of Cooper et al.'s READMEs are not files, so the true share lacking a file is larger.

**C2.10 — QUALIFIED.** Line 324: "code not always well-annotated". The median annotation score is 7 of 10, range 1 to 10 (p. 1960), so the statement is true. Cooper et al. warns that this variable was "less consistent among data recorders" (p. 1958). The sentence lacks a verb ("code was not always").

**C2.11 — FALSE.** Line 324: they "found that ... code was not always reproducible (e.g., due to hard-coded file paths)". Cooper et al. did not test this. They did not run code, and they say of completeness that it is "not verified reproducibility" (p. 1960). Hard-coded paths appear only as a possibility in their Discussion: "other factors are likely to impact the ability to reuse code, such as hard-coded paths" (p. 1961). The term does not occur in the protocol or in the coders' comments. **Correction:** "They note that other factors, such as hard-coded paths, are likely to limit reuse."

**C2.12 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 324: "These findings strongly suggest that it would be beneficial if data and code is reviewed before a manuscript is published." Cooper et al. makes the same recommendation (data and code editors), which can be cited.

**C2.13 — QUALIFIED.** Line 326: "Some journals manually check data and code before an article is published. This practice is most common in economics journals, where a dedicated Data Editor oversees the reproduction of results". The American Economic Association's process is confirmed: since 2019 its Data Editor's team reviews conditionally accepted papers at eight journals (<https://news.cornell.edu/node/313496>). The report cited (Vilhuber and Cavanagh, 2025) could not be opened automatically. "Most common in economics" is a comparison across fields, for which no source was found. **Correction:** "This practice is well established in economics" unless a comparison is cited.

**C2.14 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 326: "Manual checks are laborious and delay the publication process." The first part is supported by the scale of that work. The second has no citation.

**C2.15 — QUALIFIED.** Line 326: SIVACOR is "the Scalable Infrastructure for Validation of Computational Social Science Research ... pilot project by the data editors of the American Economic Association" that "examines whether it is possible to automatically verify". The name is confirmed by Lars Vilhuber's talk page (<https://lars.vilhuber.com/talks/2026-04-29-worldbank/>), which describes a framework that lets users "confirm and demonstrate reproducible analysis". Vilhuber is the Association's Data Editor. The page says neither "pilot" nor that the Association's editors run it, and it has no citation in the manuscript. **Correction:** cite the page and write "a project led by the Data Editor of the American Economic Association", after confirming with the source.

**C2.16 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 326: "The extent to which automated processes can reduce the workload ... is an open question."

**C2.17 — TRUE.** Line 328: Metacheck is "a novel open source tool". The source is public at `scienceverse/metacheck`, and "checks best practices" matches the package's description.

**C2.18 — TRUE.** Line 328: Cooper et al.'s data are available at the GitHub address given, `nhcooper123/reproduce-reuse-recycle`. The repository exists and holds them, and the article cites the same address and the Zenodo record.

**C2.19 — TRUE.** Line 328: "145 people coded a median of 10 (min = 1, max = 68) manuscripts". The numbers follow from `recorder_ID`, except that a recorder ID may be a pair (C1.3). **Correction:** "145 recorders".

**C2.20 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 328: "the human coders exerted considerable effort".

**C2.21 — QUALIFIED.** Line 328: "coding papers published between 2017 and 2024 on eight questions per paper". Cooper et al. (p. 1956) has eight numbered headings, but says: "Rather than list each question in our protocol ... we have grouped questions thematically". The form has many more questions. **Correction:** "eight groups of questions", also at lines 330 and 332.

**C2.22 — TRUE.** Line 328: the list of what was coded, from use and archiving to DOI and licence, matches headings 1 to 8 on pp. 1956-1957.

**C2.23 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 330: a tool at comparable accuracy "would substantially reduce the workload".

**C2.24 — FALSE.** Line 330: "their trained human coders". Cooper et al. does not report any training. Participants "randomly selected papers" and "followed a bespoke protocol", with a chat channel for questions (p. 1956), and the protocol shows volunteers working from instructions. **Correction:** "their human coders", also at line 1031.

**C2.25 — TRUE.** Line 330: Metacheck "uses text search, rule-based classification, API's, and optional large language models". The package has all of these (`llm()`, `llm_use()`). The plural should be "APIs".

**C2.26 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 330: the three modules "closely resemble the classifications that Cooper et al. asked their human coders to perform". It is true for presence, location, download and README, but not for licence scoping or for usefulness.

**C2.27 — FALSE.** Line 332: "for each of the eight questions in their protocol, we summarize what Cooper et al. found, and examine whether that question can currently be automated". The manuscript's numbered sections stop at question 3, and later sections treat data availability, licences (part of question 8), README (question 5) and annotation (question 7). Questions 4 (file extensions) and 6 (completeness) are not examined, and DOI (question 8) is not reported. **Correction:** either add file formats and DOI, which Metacheck's columns allow, or write "for the questions that can be compared". Lines 858 and 1023 already say that some have no counterpart.

**C2.28 — QUALIFIED.** Line 332: "we use Cooper et al.'s openly archived data as ground truth". The citation is correct. But the manuscript itself shows the coders were wrong in many disagreements, and Cooper et al. reports 91.7% mean recorder agreement (p. 1958). The phrase "ground truth" (also lines 862, 984, 990, 1023) conflicts with those findings. **Suggested wording:** "as the reference".

**C2.29 — QUALIFIED.** Line 332: "The results generated by Metacheck are completely automated, do not rely on AI, and can be reproduced by re-running the code, without any human input." "Do not rely on AI" holds: `code/run_metacheck.R` never enables a language model. "Without human input" is too strong: the run has settings chosen by hand (higher download budgets for two papers, one paper excluded on the author's decision), and needs keys and Docker. Re-running also depends on live repositories, and 191 papers were rerun after failures such as HTTP 429 (Appendix A.8), so identical results cannot be promised. The verdicts, audits and categories are human or AI judgements, as stated elsewhere. **Correction:** "the module results are produced without a language model and without judgement per paper; they depend on the repositories' state at the time."

**C2.30 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 332: "Unlike a validation study that reports a single accuracy percentage, our goal here is ...".

**C2.31 — QUALIFIED.** Line 334: "Metacheck follows FAIR principles, which state that 'all research objects should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) both for machines and for people' [p. 3]." The quotation and page are correct (Wilkinson et al., 2016, PDF page 3). But that sentence reports the conclusion of the meeting that led to the principles, and it does not state the principles. A tool also does not "follow" them; it uses data shared according to them. **Correction:** "Metacheck relies on data and code being shared according to the FAIR principles, the idea being that ...".

**C2.32 — QUALIFIED.** Line 334: "if authors state that the data is shared in a PDF file shared as supplementary material the data is not FAIR, because a machine can't find or access the datafile". The conclusion is the manuscript's definition and is reasonable. The reason is too strong: a supplementary file usually has an address. What fails is that a table in a PDF is not machine-readable and carries no persistent identifier of its own. **Correction:** state these two reasons.

**C2.33 — TRUE.** Line 334: "Cooper and colleagues did not limit their coding to FAIR data". The protocol counts data "mentioned in the data availability statement, or supplementary materials", and 23 papers have that label.

**C2.34 — TRUE.** Line 334: "Metacheck will always miss some information that human coders found", as a consequence of C2.33. In the audit, 115 papers fall here.

**C2.35 — TRUE.** Line 334: "the Dryad data repository requires a CC0-1.0 license at deposit for every dataset with no author choice involved". Dryad's requirements page says: "Dryad does not accept any files with licensing terms that are incompatible with the Creative Commons Zero waiver", and refers to "the CC0 license waiver required for publication" (<https://datadryad.org/requirements>). The only choice offered is hosting software on Zenodo.

**C2.36 — FALSE.** Line 334: "Metacheck retrieves this information, but the human coders were unable to locate license information by visually examining the Dryad repository." The coders mostly did find it. Among papers where Metacheck names Dryad as a data platform, Cooper et al. coded a licence as "Yes" in 922, "No" in 27, "Unsure" in 6, and left 37 blank. Cooper et al. reports CC0 for 1076 papers and calls it "the licence used by Dryad" (p. 1960). **Root:** a generalisation from the disagreements, which are the only cases reviewed. **Correction:** "In 46 papers coders recorded no licence where the repository's metadata has one, in 26 of which the comment names Dryad."

## Methods

**C3.1 — QUALIFIED.** Line 338: "We obtained the list of paper DOIs, journals, and years directly from the cleaned dataset". True, except that four DOIs in the dataset are wrong and were corrected (`cooper_doi_corrections()`). The independent join on paper number gives the same mapping for all 1861 rows, which confirms the correction. **Correction:** mention it.

**C3.2 — QUALIFIED.** Line 338: "downloaded all articles through an R script". This script is not in the repository, and `data/bes.rds` is kept private for copyright reasons. Column `source` of `data/papers_data.csv` records downloads from Europe PMC and through a Wiley proxy. At least one paper's text is the PubMed Central author manuscript (10.1111/1365-2656.12794), which lacks the data section, so "all articles" were not all in the published form. **Correction:** say where the texts came from, and either add the script or say it is not shared.

**C3.3 — FALSE.** Line 338: "using GROBID 9.0". All 1861 papers carry `input_format` "grobid 0.9.0". **Root:** a typing error. **Correction:** "GROBID 0.9.0".

**C3.4 — TRUE.** Line 338: the descriptions of `repo_check`, `data_check` and `code_check`, including that `code_check` "checks R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB code files". This repeats the module's documentation (`code_check.R`, line 7, and `listed_langs`). In this corpus only R, Python, MATLAB and Mplus files occur; Cooper et al.'s coded languages also list no Stata, SAS or SPSS. "To mirror to manual coding" should read "to mirror the manual coding".

**C3.5 — QUALIFIED.** Line 338: "we ran the `reproducibility_check` module to illustrate additional benefits of automation". The module was run (`repro_*` columns), but the main text no longer reports it; it is in Appendix A.7. **Correction:** add "(see the Appendix)".

## Section 1: use and archiving

**C4.1 — TRUE.** Line 595: the quotation beginning "Of the 1861 papers in our dataset". It is verbatim from Cooper et al., p. 1958 (apart from spaces around the equals signs), and the manuscript gives no page. **Correction:** add the page.

**C4.2 — TRUE.** Line 595: "The first two percentages are based on text in data availability statements and the method section." Cooper et al., p. 1956: "We used the Data Availability statement to determine whether data were used and archived", and for code "we read the Methods section".

**C4.3 — TRUE.** Line 595: "There are tools that automatically check data availability statements, such as OddPub". OddPub reads a paper's text for data and code sharing (Riedel et al., 2020). It searches the full text, not only the statement.

**C4.4 — TRUE.** Line 595: `open_practices` "reads the full text and judges from the wording alone". Its code is a set of text patterns over the paper (`open_practices.R`). "Equivalent" is fair in purpose.

**C4.5 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 595: "These automated checks most closely follow the coding by Cooper and colleagues".

**C4.6 — TRUE.** Line 595: `repo_check` "classifies data and code as available based on a linked repository that can be automatically accessed through an API". This is correct in substance. Data and code classification itself is done by `data_check` and `code_check`.

**C4.7 — QUALIFIED.** Line 599: "The Metacheck Open Practices module does the same, but is intentionally over-inclusive". The module's documentation says "a lower false negative rate, but also a higher false positive rate" than ODDPub, and the patterns are broad. The results agree: sensitivity 86% against 80%, specificity 9% against 45%. The word "intentionally" is an inference. The module's author could confirm it.

**C4.8 — TRUE.** Line 599: the description of the comparison: "Yes" (and for data "Yes, but not all files") as open, and ambiguous or blank answers excluded. It matches `build_master_comparison()`. Also true: "`data_open`/`code_open` were only asked for papers Cooper and colleagues had already coded as archiving". In the file every non-blank `data_open` has `data_availability` "Yes".

**C4.9 — TRUE.** Line 599: `open_practices` has "higher sensitivity ... but lower specificity" than OddPub for data, and "the difference was larger" for code. Accuracy differs by 6 points for data and 33 for code.

**C4.10 — FALSE.** Line 599: "Both tools, in other words, are much more likely to say a paper shares open data or code than to say it does not". It holds for data (80% and 86% say open) and for `open_practices` on code among the rated papers (77%). It fails for OddPub on code: among the 498 rated papers it says open for 44%, and over the whole corpus 15%. Over the corpus `open_practices` says open code for 40%. **Root:** a generalisation from the data results. **Correction:** "For data, both tools say open for most papers. For code, `open_practices` does so for 77% of the rated papers and OddPub for 44%."

**C4.11 — TRUE.** Line 599: "very few papers the human coders judged as clearly *not* sharing (11 for data, 3 for code), so the specificity estimates ... should be treated as indicative". The numbers are correct. With 3 papers the estimates are not even indicative.

**C4.12 — QUALIFIED.** Line 599: "neither distinguishes between data and code repositories". Both give separate answers for data and for code, from the wording, so a reader could misread this. They do not inspect repositories at all. **Correction:** "neither inspects a repository".

**C4.13 — TRUE.** Line 601: "OddPub and `open_practices` classify every paper". Neither column has a missing value. The later counts are verified in Part 1, and their labels match the file ("Needs specific software or too large", "Maybe if I had the right software").

**C4.14 — FALSE.** Line 605: "in total, 1789 papers contain a link to a repository with either data or code." 1789 is the number of papers coded as sharing data or code, and not all give a repository: the audit finds 18 with no repository cited, and 23 papers have the label "Supplementary materials". **Correction:** "in total, 1789 papers were coded as archiving data or code."

**C4.15 — TRUE.** Line 605: "Metacheck found 1561 papers that contained a link to a repository in the main text where it could verify that the repository contained files." `files_n` above zero, and detection excludes the reference list (`include_refs = FALSE`).

**C4.16 — QUALIFIED.** Line 605: "1487 papers contained data, 452 papers contained code, and 1532 papers contained either data or code according to `repo_check`". The numbers are right, but the classification comes from `data_check` and `code_check`. **Correction:** name them.

**C4.17 — QUALIFIED.** Line 605: "17 papers where Metacheck found data or code while Cooper's coders missed it". The 17 is right, but "missed" is not established. Nine have no verdict at all, because the coders answered that the paper used no data, so that column was not compared. Of the others, two have a verdict that the coders were right on data availability, and one rests on another author's repository. **Correction:** "17 papers where Metacheck found files it classified as data or code while the coders recorded none."

**C4.18 — TRUE.** Line 607: Metacheck supports "Dataverse, DSpace 6 and 7, Figshare, and DataOne, and dedicated support for OSF, Zenodo, ResearchBox, Dryad, ReShare, GitHub, GitLab, Mendeley Data, FSD, AsPredicted, and 4TU". Functions exist for each (for example `.rbox_info` for ResearchBox, `researchdata4tu_info` for 4TU).

**C4.19 — FALSE.** Line 607: "Metacheck supports over 285 unique repositories (...76 Figshare-based hosts...)". The correct numbers are 41 Figshare-based hosts and 250 repositories. See the explanation in Part 1. "Over" is also wrong: the count is exact.

**C4.20 — TRUE.** Line 607: "this is only a subset of all repositories used in manuscripts". 101 papers use FAIR repositories outside it.

## Section 1: why Metacheck missed data or code

**C5.1 — QUALIFIED.** Line 754: "We reviewed the 274 papers ... by checking the contents of the repository." Many have no repository to check (18), or one that is not reachable. Each was read by an AI agent, as the code comment in `full-317-audit-load` says; 227 rows state that they were then checked "by comparison, not by a full rerun". The manuscript's text never tells the reader that this review was made by AI agents, although line 797 says so for another review. **Correction:** state who or what performed it, because "we reviewed" suggests a human.

**C5.2 — TRUE.** Line 754: "five reasons". The clusters are mutually exclusive and sum to 274, by a check in the chunk.

**C5.3 — TRUE.** Line 754: "In 18 papers we found no reference to a repository ... either explicitly withheld for confidentiality, ethical, or Indigenous-data-sovereignty reasons, could not be shared for legal reasons, or were in shared in the paper or its supplemental material. **C5.4 — QUALIFIED.** Line 754: these papers are counted among those where coders "found data or code". For withheld data, the coders' "Yes" is itself an error: several of these statements say the data are not available. Line 876 treats this group as errors by the coders. The group is therefore better described as "where the coders coded data or code as shared". This also affects the sentence on 1674 papers (C5.19).

**C5.5 — QUALIFIED.** Line 754: "In 81 papers the citation or the repository did not meet basic FAIR requirements, so no automated tool could have retrieved the data." The count is right. "No automated tool" is too strong for a repository that blocks automated requests (7) or was temporarily not live (14). What the audit shows is that Metacheck could not, and that the repository does not offer machine access. **Correction:** "so that a tool using the repository's API cannot retrieve the data".

**C5.6 — TRUE.** Line 754: the five subgroups (5 private links, 2 organisation pages, 7 blocks, 14 not live, 53 without an API). The counts follow from the audit file, and sample rows match their label (for example DIGITAL.CSIC blocking requests).

**C5.7 — TRUE.** Line 754: "Automated access to repositories has become harder in recent years because of heavy scraping of files, which repository managers assume is mostly done by bots collecting training data". **C5.8 — QUALIFIED.** Line 754: "In a 2025 survey, over 90% of responding repositories reported aggressive bot traffic, often causing slowdowns or outages, and many responded with rate limits and other blocks". **C5.9 — TRUE.** Line 754: "We observed this directly when attempting to download files". The audit has 7 papers with blocked repositories, and Appendix A.8 records HTTP 429 refusals during the corpus run. These refusals show access limits, not that bots were the cause.

FAIR status rests on the audit's agent judgement. A group not among the examples is NCBI's databases, mentioned in 18 rows. **Suggested addition:** name it.

**C5.11 — QUALIFIED.** Line 756: these repositories "occur less frequently in the published literature". For one journal family, 101 papers is 6% of those with data or code, and no comparison with other platforms is made. The statement is plausible but unmeasured.

Their stated observation is about code: "60% of code files that are hosted on GitHub or similar are also archived on Zenodo" (p. 1959). For data, the file also has more than one label per paper (1782 labels on 1670 papers), but the article does not remark on it. "As on" should be "and". **Correction:** "data or code".

**C6.3 — TRUE.** Line 770: "Github is not a stable repository, while Zenodo is." Zenodo issues a persistent DOI for a fixed record. A GitHub repository can be changed or deleted: one in this corpus no longer exists (code category "GitHub repository named in the paper no longer exists"). Cooper et al. makes the same distinction, and notes that the BES policy "does not allow archiving at GitHub (or similar) alone" (p. 1959), which could be cited. The name is written "GitHub".

**C6.4 — UNVERIFIED.** Line 770: "We observed this directly, as files in some GitHub repositories changed between our first run and the final run." Nothing in this repository records it. The 12 causes in `data/review/result_change_causes_data.csv` that explain differences between the earlier and the final results are all changes in Metacheck or settings, and none is a changed repository. **To settle:** compare the earlier and final file lists of the GitHub repositories, and confirm a change with the repository's commit history. Otherwise, use the deleted repository of C6.3 as the example.

**C6.5 — QUALIFIED.** Line 770: "Cooper et al. report Dryad as the dominant data repository in ecology (57%, n = 1022), with Figshare (9%), Zenodo (12%), and 'various institutional and government repositories' (17%)", p. 1959. Two details differ: the study covers BES journals, not ecology, and the percentages are of "data files" in their words, in fact of the 1782 platform labels. **Correction:** "in these journals".

**C6.6 — TRUE.** Line 772: the two sides code as stated. Cooper et al. codes data and code separately and allows several platforms; Metacheck "lists whether files in all repositories it finds contain data and/or code files". The mapping is in `repo_url_platform()`, and "Supplementary materials" and "Personal website" are not used by Metacheck.

**C6.7 — QUALIFIED.** Line 772: "We then classify agreement (perfect, partial, or none)." The table has five categories: same platforms, Metacheck lists fewer, Metacheck lists more, each lists one the other lacks, no shared platform. **Correction:** name these.

**C6.8 — FALSE.** Line 795: "Most of the differences are caused by the previously discussed limitations in the repositories that Metacheck supports. Of the 137 differences for data, 52 are cases where Metacheck lists more, which is not a limitation of support. Of the 55 where it lists fewer, 38 involve "Other repo/database" and 27 of those also have Dryad. Others are Dryad with Zenodo (4) and GitHub with Zenodo (11), both supported platforms. **Root:** one frequent pattern was written up as the description of the whole group. **Correction:** "In 55 papers Metacheck lists fewer platforms than the coders. In 38 of these the platform it misses is 'Other repo/database', in 27 of them beside a Dryad deposit." Replace "Most of the differences" with a sentence that names both directions. Some addresses are not repositories but pages inside one, such as an issue or a file. **Correction:** "215 links to GitHub and GitLab", "31 of these links".

**C6.10 — TRUE.** Line 797: "Metacheck cannot yet differentiate between data or code that authors created and shared, and data or code that they reused, and it treats all files in repositories linked to in a manuscript as the paper's own". **C6.11 — QUALIFIED.** Line 797: "Cooper and colleagues did not code this either." No column records it, so this is true for the file. The protocol says it wants data "generated as part of the project" as well as collations, and code "vital for reproducing the analyses". **C6.13 — TRUE.** Line 797: "With one exception these hold software or scripts the authors used, not reused data; the exception is the repository of a text corpus, linked to by 2 papers." All 31 reasons in the file were read, and they agree. The corpus is the Standardized Project Gutenberg Corpus.

Three papers in the corpus have such an address in their text, so the conversion or the download route altered them. It is recorded in the project's notes as not traced.

The sentence also has a grammatical gap: "whether data download and code archiving".

The manuscript prints no confusion table. McNemar's test appears only for data availability and licences, and sensitivity and specificity in the text only for four. **Root:** tables and tests were removed, and this sentence was not. **Correction:** describe what is reported, or add a table of counts. The summary table can hold these.

Also, comments often name only one or two of these sources. **Correction:** "against the evidence each comment names".

**C9.4 — TRUE.** Line 862: three verdicts with the given meaning, and for README a fourth, `DIFFERENT_DEFINITION`. "Most often because the paper cites more than one repository" holds for the 54 `BOTH_DEFENSIBLE` verdicts on platforms, which are most of the 58.

**C9.5 — FALSE.** Line 862: "every case an earlier round had marked as unclear ... was settled in a final review (15 October 2026) ... (`code/03_comparing_results/review_2026-10-15/`)". The 15 October review was not the last: the file has verdicts stamped 17, 18 and 31 October and 1 November. **Root:** the text was written before the repository was rebuilt and before later rechecks. **Correction:** "settled in later reviews, the last on 1 November 2026; the verdicts and comments are in `data/review/disagreement_review_data.xlsx`".

**C9.6 — TRUE.** Line 862: "Two rules decide what Metacheck is expected to find: only a README *file* counts as a README ..., and a file listing the variables of a data file is a codebook". The idea it describes, carrying a verdict forward when both answers are unchanged, is still how the worklist works. **Root:** history of the earlier repository. **Correction:** replace with a short description of the final process, which Appendix A.11 gives.

## Comment count and comment quality

**C13.1 — TRUE.** Line 902: `code_annotation_scale`, "coded for 543 of the 1861 papers", and `code_check` records `comment_lines`, `code_lines` and `percentage_comment`. The columns exist, and 543 follows from the file.

**C13.2 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 902: if a line count tracked the rating, the rating "adds comparatively little"; if not, coders "are picking up on something a mechanical count cannot see". This is the reasoning behind the comparison.

**C13.3 — TRUE.** Line 918: comment lines are divided by "total lines", over all files with counts. The code divides by the sum of comment and code lines, which amounts to the same up to the handling of blank lines.

**C13.4 — FALSE.** Line 918: "the smaller overlap reflects that Metacheck's count requires at least one code file to have actually downloaded and parsed". This is not the main reason. Of 452 papers with code in Metacheck's table, 450 have counts, so failed downloads and parsing cost 2 papers. The overlap is 389 of 543 because Metacheck found no code for 152 of the rated papers, for the reasons given in the code section, and 2 others have code without counts. **Correction:** "the smaller overlap reflects that Metacheck found no code for 152 of the rated papers."

**C13.5 — TRUE.** Line 920: "The correlation is weak but not zero", with the printed values. Both computations agree.

**C13.6 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 920: the raw count "gives essentially the same result ... so this is not an artifact of how the percentage was computed" (0.14 against 0.17), and the negative correlation of length with percentage (-0.30) is "not something that would by itself explain" the weak correlation. The numbers are correct, and these are interpretations.

**C13.7 — QUALIFIED.** Line 922: "a paper's comment *density* is a poor stand-in for a human coder's *quality* judgment". True for these data, with one omission. Cooper et al. warns that annotation quality was "less consistent among data recorders": the same paper received ratings from 2 to 10 (p. 1958). A rating that varies this much between raters limits any correlation with it. **Correction:** add this, which weakens the conclusion that the count does not track annotation quality.

**C13.8 — FALSE.** Line 922: "A single well-placed sentence explaining a complex analysis counts as excellent annotation on Cooper et al.'s scale". Their scale runs from "1=not annotated at all" to "10=thorough annotation throughout" (p. 1957). A single sentence would not reach the top of it. **Correction:** "Comments that restate the code count as heavy annotation by line count, whereas few but informative comments count little", without a statement on their scale.

**C13.9 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 922: boilerplate "would plausibly score poorly", and a language-model classifier "could more plausibly approximate" content, with validation.

## Discussion: what should change

**C15.1 — TRUE.** Line 984: text extraction from PDF "has known limitations which lead to broken or undetected links to repositories". 30 papers in the audit show this. "PDF files are created to optimize human readability" is a general description.

**C15.2 — QUALIFIED.** Line 984: "(e.g., see CITE https://github.com/scienceverse/bibr/releases/tag/v0.6.0)". The release exists (30 September 2026). The word CITE is a placeholder for a reference, and the same holds for `ms_FAIR_data_and_code`, which also exists. **Correction:** add both to `references.bib`.

**C15.3 — TRUE.** Line 984: publishers could share machine-readable XML "as for example PLOSone already does". A PLOS ONE article's file address returned `application/xml` when tested. The journal is written "PLOS ONE".

**C15.4 — QUALIFIED.** Line 984: "our review shows that many institutional repositories need repository-specific development work (see the Metacheck limitation cluster above)". The cluster named holds text conversion and defects on platforms already supported. The evidence for this claim is in the group "FAIR, on an unsupported platform", 101 papers. **Correction:** change the reference.

**C15.5 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 984: tools should support all FAIR repositories and formats; researchers, journals and repositories should do what is listed; Metacheck can assist, "as the current manuscript demonstrates".

**C15.6 — FALSE.** Line 984: "The Dryad repository is not accessible without an API key, and even then allows only a very limited number of API requests". Without a key, Dryad's dataset, version and file-listing API answers: tested on 1 November 2026 with HTTP 200, and Metacheck's own message says listings and metadata "can be read without one". What needs a key is the file contents: a request without one returned HTTP 401, also tested. On limits, Dryad's documentation says an API account lets one "access the API at higher rates", without a number that was found. The appendix records HTTP 429 during the run. **Correction:** "Dryad's API returns metadata without a key, but file contents require one, even for public datasets, and requests are limited in rate, which slows automated checks."

**C15.7 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 984: "Researchers are recommended to share data in fully machine accessible repositories, such as Zenodo, instead." The advice follows from C15.6. Readers should also learn that Appendix A.5 records Zenodo faults, and that most BES data are on Dryad, whose deposits the society has sponsored (<https://jecologyblog.com/2014/01/20/journal-of-ecology-is-part-of-new-bes-data-archiving-policy/>).

**C15.8 — TRUE.** Line 984: "Some repositories do not yet have an API". 53 papers in the audit, by its judgement.

**C15.9 — FALSE.** Line 986: "Registries of data repositories exist (e.g., https://www.re3data.org) but the registry does not contain information about the APIs used by each repository." re3data records this. The record for Dryad, requested through its own API on 1 November 2026, holds `<r3d:api apiType="REST">https://datadryad.org/api/v2/docs/</r3d:api>`. **Root:** presumably an impression from the website. **Correction:** "re3data records APIs for repositories that report them, but not whether a tool can use them." This could be useful for adding support.

**C15.10 — TRUE.** Line 986: "Some repositories disappear, and new ones are added." 14 papers point to repositories not live or not accessible when checked, and one GitHub repository no longer exists.

**C15.11 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 986: support is straightforward with an established API and needs more effort with a unique one. This matches Metacheck's code, with families of hosts and 11 dedicated platforms. It seems likely that large repositories will be more findable. Dryad is named here as more findable, shortly after being named as hard to access (C15.6), and these two could be reconciled.

For the two platform rows only agreement is given (C1.7). The column heading "Cooper caught, MC missed" also reads badly for README: its 95.1% includes the 294 papers where the coders coded a README or metadata and no README file exists, so nothing was missed. **Correction:** "Cooper yes, MC no" and "MC yes, Cooper no".

The code sets a paper with no repository to FALSE, as described. This compares with a value the reader has not seen. **Correction:** delete, as in C10.2.

**C16.4 — TRUE.** Line 1019: `code_download` has one disagreement (100%, 0%), and `data_download` has "only 2 codeable Cooper-`No` cases, too few for its specificity". These hold. The same caution applies to `code_download`, with 1 case.

**C16.5 — FALSE.** Line 1019: "`code_archived` shows the most pronounced asymmetry of any boolean construct (sensitivity 71.2%, specificity 96.7%)". The gap is 25.5 points. Those of the others are: `any_readme` 31.0, `data_availability` 42.2, `data_license` 72.9, and `data_download` and `code_download` higher still, with almost no negative cases. Taken as the share of disagreements in one direction, it is 82% against 95% for README and 90% for data availability. **Root:** written when other values were different. **Correction:** "`code_archived` has low sensitivity and high specificity", without the superlative.

**C16.6 — TRUE.** Line 1019: `code_archived` "is genuinely multi-causal, spanning code the paper does not link to directly, a repository-detection gap, and ... journal Supporting Information". These are the categories 34, 28 and 33.

**C16.7 — TRUE.** Line 1019: "`any_readme`'s asymmetry is mostly a matter of definition: in 63.0% of its disagreements Cooper et al. coded a README or metadata, and the deposit contains no README file." 294 of 467. See C12.9.

**C16.8 — TRUE.** Line 1021: "positive predictive value was above 96% for five of the six boolean constructs", with the printed values. "Rarely spurious" means rare by the coders' answer.

**C16.9 — QUALIFIED.** Discussion: `code_archived`'s lower value holds "because in 21 of its 202 disagreements `code_check` correctly found real code files ... a genuine human-coder miss, not a Metacheck false positive". The value rests on 36 such cases. In 21 the coders were wrong. In the other 15 Metacheck's Yes is a false positive: 13 counted others' software, and 2 a README. Two of these 15 are also coder errors (C7.16). The sentence gives only the first group, and it makes the lower value seem to be no fault of the tool's. **Correction:** give both numbers.

**C16.10 — TRUE.** Line 1021: "overwhelmingly a *recall* problem for most constructs". The share of disagreements where the coders found what Metacheck did not is 90%, 82%, 82% and 95% for four constructs. Licences (12%) and code download (0%) go the other way, as "most" allows.

**C16.11 — QUALIFIED.** Line 1021: "for `code_archived` specifically, a nontrivial share of Metacheck's `FALSE` answers reflect a real detection gap". This is true: the negative predictive value is 86.4%. But it does not follow from the discussion of positive values, and "specifically" is not warranted, since the same holds for data availability and README. **Correction:** remove "specifically".

**C16.12 — TRUE.** Line 1023: "Three constructs ... have no Metacheck counterpart". Usefulness, completeness and annotation (C8.12).

**C16.13 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 1023: structural questions are answered reliably and interpretive ones less so; language models are "a plausible route". Examples such as "is this repository the one holding the data" are supported by reviews, and the example of a description being a real README is a question of definition (C12.9).

## Discussion: the repository detection statement

**C17.1 — FALSE.** Line 1025: "the data-versus-code repository conflation pattern ... appears as the dominant or a substantial cause of disagreement in `data_archive`, `data_license`, and `code_archived` alike. This is not three independent bugs; it is one architectural gap". The current review does not support it. In `data_license`, the scoping appears in 2 of 8 `COOPER_RIGHT` verdicts. In `code_archived`, none of the 21 reasons in the classification of 203 is of this kind. In `data_archive`, the categories are of a different kind (C6.8). The review has no such category, and the code does not contain a single assumption of "the" repository: it uses all repositories. **Root:** a summary of an early stage of review. **Correction:** delete the passage. It is also followed by "It remains ... the single largest reason", which refers to something else, namely non-detection.

**C17.2 — FALSE.** Line 1025: "a paper's own text names a real, working DOI on a mainstream platform (overwhelmingly Dryad, Zenodo, or Figshare), and `repo_check` never queries it at all." This contradicts line 876, and the evidence supports line 876. Of the 175 papers in this group, the coders labelled 136 "Other repo/database", and only 32 are labelled Dryad, Figshare or Zenodo alone. In the audit, 122 are on platforms Metacheck does not support. **Root:** an early stage, before those platforms were reviewed. **Correction:** "a paper's text names a repository, most often on a platform Metacheck does not support".

**C17.3 — TRUE.** Line 1025: repository non-detection "accounts for 175 of `data_availability`'s 227 `COOPER_RIGHT` disagreements and 96 of `any_readme`'s 156". The counts come from text patterns (Part 1), and all 175 appear in the audit. The audit was not matched for the 96.

**C17.4 — TRUE.** Line 1025: "For code it is a smaller cause, accounting for 28 of `code_archived`'s 167 ..., behind code on Zenodo that the paper does not link to directly (34) and code provided only as journal Supporting Information (33)."

**C17.5 — TRUE.** Line 1025: "These two causes lie in how authors share code, so changes to Metacheck would not resolve them." For the first group, a tool could follow Dryad's related works, but under the manuscript's definition this would not count as a direct link.

**C17.6 — JUDGEMENT.** Line 1025: fixing the gaps "at the level of how Metacheck decides which repository 'counts'" "would likely resolve a meaningful fraction". Given C17.1 and C17.2, what would help is support for more platforms, since 122 of the 175 are of that kind.

## Discussion: history of defects

**C18.1 — FALSE.** Line 1027: "Twelve individual software defects identified over the course of this project were reported upstream, fixed, and reverified against a full corpus rerun". The count is out of date. The appendix's headings alone give 5 in A.1, 5 in A.3, 7 in A.5, 3 in A.6 and 3 in A.8, and it describes more. Not all are fixed: #505 is open, and the manuscript itself reports others as remaining. **Root:** the number dates from A.5. **Correction:** give a count from the appendix, or write "Defects found were reported", citing it.

**C18.2 — TRUE.** Line 1027: the five issues (#379, #380, #378, #383, #384) exist and were closed on 6 September 2026, and their descriptions match. #384's title concerns a failed fetch, and the truncation cause is reported in its comments and in Appendix A.1.

**C18.3 — FALSE.** Line 1027: agreement on `data_download` "rose from 93.5% to 99.1%" through the fix of #379. Appendix A.1 says "disagreed on 51 of 967 comparable papers (94.7% agreement); after it, agreement rose to 99.1% (908/916 papers...)", and 51 of 967 is indeed 94.7%. The figure of 93.5% occurs in `numbers_audit.md` of the earlier repository. Neither can be recomputed from the final results, as they describe earlier runs. **Root:** two stages of the project were recorded separately. **Correction:** use 94.7% with the appendix's counts, or delete the figures, since the body should report the final results.

**C18.4 — TRUE.** Line 1027: `code_download` rose "from 66.2% ... to 89.7% ... to 97.2%", "the largest of any construct", and it is now 99.8%, with 1 disagreement. The 32,768-byte limit is in the appendix and the issue. The values before 99.8% are historical.

**C18.5 — QUALIFIED.** Line 1029: "A further seven fixes ... Six of the seven had not; the seventh — the R-package-source-tree exclusion". The appendix's A.5 counts two for Zenodo, three for platforms and two for rate limits, which leaves no place for the exclusion as a separate fix, and its opening paragraph says "five more fixes". A rerun of the other 868 papers is described, supporting the check. "Six of the seven had not" broken anything has no record to test. **Correction:** make the appendix consistent, and write "one of these".

**C18.6 — QUALIFIED.** Line 1029: the account of the 16 repositories repeats lines 868 and 870 almost word for word, with the same caution about `phylomice` (C9.10). **Correction:** keep one.

**C18.7 — QUALIFIED.** Line 1031: "Appendix A documents, in full detail, every defect ...; the body of this manuscript reports only the current, post-fix numbers." The appendix is now a separate document, titled "Appendix". The body does report earlier numbers, in the paragraph before this one. "Trained human coder" appears here (C2.24). The evaluation of the approach as "the more useful contribution" is a judgement. **Correction:** delete the second clause, and update the reference.
